what: Doximity runs a professional network for American doctors. Most practising physicians have an account, and they use it to communicate with colleagues, send secure messages, hold telehealth visits and read medical news. Pharmaceutical companies and hospitals pay to reach those doctors.
customers: Pharmaceutical companies marketing drugs to prescribers, health systems recruiting physicians and promoting services, and medical recruiters — all paying to reach a verified audience of doctors.
money: Advertising and educational content delivered to targeted physician specialties.
Recruitment advertising for health systems and physician workflow tools.
moat: A verified network containing most American physicians cannot be rebuilt: the doctors are already there, verification is hard, and a professional network’s value to each member comes from the others being present. Pharmaceutical companies have no other way to reach a specific specialty at scale with verified identity, which is why they pay what they pay.
risks: The shares trade at about 41.1 times earnings, 26.6 times EV/EBITDA and 8.0 times sales — a full price for a business of this size.
Revenue is concentrated in pharmaceutical marketing budgets, which are cut when a drug launch is delayed or a product goes generic.
Eighteen analysts average a $31.50 target, only 6% above the current price.
Drug advertising is politically exposed, and restrictions on pharmaceutical promotion have been proposed periodically in the United States.
The addressable market is bounded by the number of American doctors, which does not grow quickly.
opportunities: A net margin of about 30% and free cash flow of $296.8M on $661.6M of revenue is exceptional profitability.
The shares trade at about 17.8 times free cash flow, with debt of only $10.2M against $219.2M of cash.
Revenue has grown every year, from $343.5M in 2022 to $644.9M in 2026.
A verified network of most American physicians is effectively impossible to replicate.
Pharmaceutical companies have no comparable way to reach a specific specialty at scale with verified identity.
watch: Revenue per customer among the largest pharmaceutical clients. The physician audience is essentially fully captured, so growth must come from each client spending more.
view: Doximity has built something that cannot be built twice. Most practising American physicians have an account, their identities are verified, and the network’s value to each member comes from the others being on it. A competitor cannot simply launch a rival — the doctors are already somewhere, verification is laborious, and nobody joins an empty network. That is a genuine and durable moat.

What makes it unusually profitable is who pays. Pharmaceutical companies need to reach specific prescribing specialties — the cardiologists, the oncologists, the rheumatologists who will write a particular drug — and verified identity at scale is the thing they cannot get anywhere else. They pay accordingly, which is why a company with $662 million of revenue earns a roughly 30% net margin and generates $297 million of free cash flow against almost no debt. These are software economics on an advertising business.

The ceiling is the problem, and it is a hard one. There are a finite number of American doctors, Doximity has essentially all of them, and that number does not grow quickly. So growth cannot come from adding members; it must come from each pharmaceutical client spending more per year. That is achievable for a while — more formats, more specialties, more of each client’s budget — and it is not an unlimited runway. Revenue per large client is the number that tells you how much is left.

At 41 times earnings and 26.6 times EV/EBITDA with eighteen analysts seeing 6% of upside, the market has correctly identified an excellent business and priced it as one. The risk that gets too little attention is political: pharmaceutical advertising is periodically a target of American political argument, and restrictions on drug promotion would hit three-quarters of this company’s revenue directly. That is a low-probability, high-impact exposure sitting underneath a premium multiple, and at this price I would want a discount for it rather than none.
bull: Pharmaceutical clients keep shifting budget to the only verified physician network at scale, revenue per client rises, and 30% margins compound with almost no capital.
bear: The physician audience is fully captured so growth must come from client budgets, pharmaceutical marketing spending tightens, and a 41 times multiple derates.
